title: Identify the positive inertia decrease
spoken: The positive inertial mass decrease equals L divided by c squared.
explanation: Matching the low-speed drop to the Newtonian form one half times the mass decrease times v squared identifies L/c². This coefficient identification needs the low-speed limit and the unchanged-offset premise; it is not obtained by assuming a body energy mc².
assumptions: Two equal, opposite light pulses remove total positive energy L; their symmetry removes recoil in the body’s rest frame.
The two inertial descriptions refer to the same emission and the same body boundary; |v| < c.
These are authored modern teaching equations, not a transcription or printed-notation concordance.
The relation H − E = K + C uses the same unknown additive C before and after emission. This is a premise; conservation and subtraction do not prove it.
The Newtonian low-speed kinetic-energy coefficient is one half m times v squared.
The mass decrease is identified from the analytic v → 0 limit, not by equating the finite-speed proxy with that limit.

notes.title: Positive decrease in inertia
notes.explanation: The positive amount by which the body’s inertial mass decreases. It is identified from the limiting low-speed coefficient, using the Newtonian kinetic-energy premise.

notes.title: Emitted energy L
notes.explanation: Total energy of both opposite pulses, in the body’s rest frame. It is not the body’s unknown total energy.

notes.title: Modern SI speed of light
notes.explanation: c denotes the speed of light in modern SI notation. A normalized model with c = 1 is a different unit convention and cannot supply values labeled metres per second.

notes.title: Convert energy units to mass units
notes.explanation: Dividing joules by square metres per square second gives kilograms. This SI factor is separate from a rounded historical cgs conversion.

notes.title: Read the limiting coefficient
notes.explanation: After matching the common one half v² factor at low speed, L/c² is the positive mass-decrease coefficient. Neither absolute body mass is supplied.
